About This Part
Volume 6D moves from infrastructure and data platforms into modern application execution. It explains
how teams package software as immutable container images, operate services on Amazon ECS and
Amazon EKS, use AWS Fargate to remove host management, build event-driven functions with AWS
Lambda, expose APIs safely, decouple systems with messaging, route domain events, and orchestrate
distributed workflows. The central engineering theme is controlled coupling. Production systems should isolate failures, scale
individual components independently, provide durable recovery paths, expose clear telemetry, and
preserve security boundaries from source code to runtime. Every chapter therefore connects service
configuration to delivery pipelines, identity, networking, observability, cost, and incident response. Scope and Safety

Chapter 31 - Amazon ECR and Container Supply-Chain Engineering
From source commit to trusted, immutable runtime artifact
Learning Objectives

Explain OCI container images, layers, manifests, tags, digests, and registries.

Design private ECR repositories, repository policies, encryption, replication, lifecycle controls, and
vulnerability scanning.

Implement immutable promotion and provenance-oriented release practices.

Authenticate Docker or compatible clients securely and troubleshoot push/pull failures.


31.1 Why the Registry Is a Security Boundary
A container registry is not merely a file store. It is the control point between software construction and
software execution. Source code becomes an image; the image becomes a deployment artifact; and the
digest identifies the exact bytes that a runtime pulls. If the registry accepts untrusted images, permits
mutable release tags, or lacks lifecycle and scanning controls, every downstream runtime inherits that
risk. Production teams therefore treat the registry as part of the software supply chain. CI systems push images,
security controls evaluate them, release automation promotes approved digests, and runtime roles receive
pull-only permissions. Human users rarely need direct push access to production repositories.

31.4 Secure Build and Promotion Pattern
Developer commit
-> CI build in isolated runner
-> unit/integration tests
-> generate SBOM and image metadata
-> push candidate image to build repository
-> vulnerability and policy gates

Promotion should move the same digest between environments rather than rebuild from the same source. Rebuilding can introduce a new base image, dependency, timestamp, or compiler output. The promoted
artifact must therefore be traceable to the source revision, build job, tests, approvals, and deployment
change record.

Interview Questions and Model Answers
1. Why should production deployments use an image digest instead of only a tag?
A digest is content-addressed and identifies the exact artifact. A tag can be moved or overwritten, so
tag-only deployment weakens reproducibility, auditability, and rollback integrity.
2. How would you separate CI and runtime permissions?
CI receives push, describe, and scan-related permissions for build repositories. Runtime execution roles
receive only the actions needed to obtain authorization and pull layers. Delete, policy, lifecycle, and
replication permissions remain administrative.
3. What belongs in a container supply-chain gate?
Source revision linkage, reproducible build metadata, tests, SBOM, vulnerability evaluation, secret
scanning, policy checks, approval evidence, signature or attestation, and digest-based promotion.
4. How do lifecycle policies create operational risk?
They can remove rollback artifacts or base layers if retention rules do not align with deployed versions,
release cadence, incident investigation, and regulatory retention. Chapter Summary

ECR is a supply-chain security boundary, not only an image store.

Tags are convenient labels; digests are deployment identities.

Separate build, promotion, runtime, and administration permissions.

Scanning, lifecycle preview, replication, audit events, and artifact provenance are production
requirements. Official AWS References

32.2 IAM Roles: Execution Versus Application
The task execution role is used by the ECS agent or Fargate platform for actions such as pulling an ECR
image, retrieving referenced secrets, and writing logs. The task role is assumed by application code inside
the container. Keeping these roles separate prevents an application from inheriting infrastructure
bootstrap privileges and enables per-service least privilege.

33.1 What Fargate Removes - and What It Does Not
AWS Fargate provides on-demand, right-sized compute capacity for containers. Teams do not provision or
patch worker instances, manage cluster packing, or scale EC2 Auto Scaling groups. The application team
still owns image security, task or pod configuration, IAM, network paths, runtime health, dependency
behavior, observability, scaling policies, and cost efficiency. You no longer manage

33.2 Sizing and Runtime Characteristics
Fargate tasks use supported CPU and memory combinations. Oversizing increases steady cost; undersizing
causes CPU throttling, memory termination, latency, and retry storms. Establish load-test profiles for
startup, steady state, bursts, garbage collection, sidecars, and failure recovery. Ephemeral storage is
temporary task storage and must not be treated as durable state.

33.3 Private Networking
A private Fargate task needs network reachability to every bootstrap and runtime dependency. Image
layers, logs, secrets, configuration, telemetry, and external APIs may require NAT or VPC endpoints. A task
that cannot reach ECR, S3-backed image layers, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, or KMS can fail before
application code starts.

40.10 Part D Interview Board
1. How would you choose between Lambda and Fargate?
Use Lambda for event-driven, short, rapidly scaling functions with supported runtime constraints. Use
Fargate when container control, longer execution, custom runtime dependencies, steady processes, or
explicit task sizing are stronger requirements.
2. How would you choose between ECS and EKS?
ECS offers simpler AWS-native orchestration. EKS provides Kubernetes APIs and ecosystem flexibility but
requires a platform operating model. The decision should follow organizational capability and workload
requirements.
3. How do you prevent asynchronous systems from hiding failure?
Define backlog-age SLOs, DLQs, execution histories, correlation IDs, business status, reconciliation, alarms,
ownership, and tested recovery paths.
4. What is the difference between retry and recovery?
Retry repeats an operation for a transient failure. Recovery restores correct business state after retries are
exhausted or outcomes are ambiguous, using DLQ repair, reconciliation, compensation, or manual
intervention.
5. Why is idempotency a cross-cutting requirement?
Queues, events, functions, workflows, networks, and external APIs can all retry. Idempotency ensures
repeated delivery or ambiguous acknowledgements do not create duplicate business outcomes.
6. What does production readiness mean for serverless?
It means controlled identity, event contracts, concurrency, dependency protection, idempotency,
retries/DLQs, observability, deployment rollback, cost limits, and runbooks - not merely absence of
servers.
